deep.reconstruction:
Folio 27 continues the table from p. 26 into p. 28. It is a table of Gaussian (addition/subtraction) logarithms in the Leonelli–Gauss form, at step 0.001.

The five columns per half-page are:
- an argument A, here 1.440–1.480 on the left and 1.480–1.520 on the right;
- B(A) = log10(1 + 10^(-A)), to 5 decimals;
- the first difference of B, in units of 10^-5;
- C(A) = A + B(A) = log10(1 + 10^A);
- the first difference of C, in units of 10^-5.

Why the differences come in complementary pairs: because C = A + B and A advances by 100 units of the fifth decimal, ΔC = 100 − |ΔB|. So the pairs 3/97 and 4/96 always sum to 100; this serves as a built-in check.

What the table is for: to find log(a+b) from log a and log b. Put A = log a − log b. Then log(a+b) = log b + C = log a + B (taking a ≥ b, so A ≥ 0). The reverse lookup serves log(a−b).

Spot checks (mine):
- A = 1.44: 10^-1.44 = 0.036308, and log10(1.036308) = 0.015489, giving 0.01549.
- A = 1.48: B = 0.014148, giving 0.01415.
- A = 1.50: 10^-1.5 = 0.0316228, and log10(1.0316228) = 0.013521, giving 0.01352.
- A = 1.52: B = 0.012921, giving 0.01292.
- Borderline cases:
  - A = 1.455: B = 0.0149719, giving 0.01497.
  - A = 1.495: B = 0.0136751, giving 0.01368.
  - A = 1.454: B = 0.015006, giving 0.01501.
  - A = 1.487: B = 0.013926, giving 0.01393.
  - A = 1.465: B = 0.0146368, giving 0.01464.

The derivative dB/dA = −10^(-A)/(1+10^(-A)) ≈ −0.035 to −0.030 over this range. That matches the tabulated differences of 4 and 3, shifting to 3 and 2 on p. 28.

C is formed simply as A + B; every sum on the page is consistent with this.
errors: No computational errors found. Spot-checked B values, including borderline roundings (1.455, 1.495, 1.454, 1.487), are correctly rounded. Every C = A + B entry is consistent, and every difference pair sums to 100.

results.what: Table of B(A)=log10(1+10^-A) and C(A)=A+B=log10(1+10^A) for A=1.440..1.520, step 0.001, 5 decimals, with first differences
results.usually_credited_to: Idea due to Z. Leonelli (1802/1803); popularized by Gauss's published table (Monatliche Correspondenz, 1812)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript computation sheet for Gauss's well-known table of addition/subtraction logarithms, which he published in 1812. It is routine tabulation that is already associated with him.

checkable.asserts: Template for regenerating the full B column for A=1.440..1.520 and comparing with the page
